sections.teaching_construction: Running case: two plates (gap H = 1 mm, plate speed U = 0.1 m/s) with water at 300 K or air at 300 K; formal model of medium, laws and geometry/boundary data; three organising questions.

sections.section: Engineering questions that need fluid mechanics
sections.lecture_material: Three engineering aspects (slide text: force on objects, force to move an object through a fluid, rate of heat/vapour transfer); cooler, dam, airplane, parachute, flow-induced oscillations, bio-fluid mechanics, washing machine, sports, Formula One; the speaker's statements on drag estimation, stents, face masks.
sections.teaching_construction: Table 1 (slide, quantity needed, statement); the qualifications on three speaker statements; hydrostatic increment rho g = 9.78 kPa/m and 0.98 MPa at 100 m as an illustration (statics taken as given).

sections.section: Flow past a cylinder: the Reynolds number and what the flow does
sections.lecture_material: Flow past a circular cylinder from the Van Dyke album: Reynolds number definition, 'non-dimensional speed'; slide captions at Re = 9.8, 13.1, 26, 28.4, 41.0, 2000, 10,000; speaker's account of eddies, release of vortices, periodic wake, unsteady force, turbulent wake and mixing.
sections.research_extension: Table 5 of Xu et al. (arXiv:2509.07192, p. 14): critical Reynolds number of the circular cylinder 46.2-47.9, mean 46.9; sensitivity to disturbances (p. 5).
sections.teaching_construction: Eq. (1.1) with unit check; Table 2 (speeds of a 1 cm cylinder in air and water for each Reynolds number); comparison of the slide's 41.0 with the tabulated critical values. Local definitions of drag, C_D with area convention and unit check, wake, separation, laminar and turbulent flow.

sections.section: Boundary layers, separation and streamlining
sections.lecture_material: Laminar and turbulent boundary layers, separation, flow past a sphere (slide text), drag crisis, bluff and streamlined bodies, relative-drag slide (F, 0.55 F, 0.075 F, 0.1 t wire), bicycle streamlining.
sections.teaching_construction: Check of the speaker's percentages against the slide values (45 %, less than 10 %, factor 13); statement that the slide's numbers have no source or Reynolds number.

sections.section: Other flow phenomena in the lecture
sections.lecture_material: Laminar and turbulent water jet, propeller and fan vortices, leapfrogging smoke rings, wingtip vortices, spinning disk and sphere, Kelvin-Helmholtz instability (tube tilted by 6 degrees).
sections.teaching_construction: Classification as a list of phenomena the continuum equations must describe; no mechanism claimed.

sections.section: What a fluid is
sections.lecture_material: Solid and fluid between plates under a force F; continuous deformation on application of a shear force; deformation rate; a fluid cannot resist a shear force; liquids and gases not distinguished; hydromechanics and aerodynamics.
sections.teaching_construction: Shear strain and strain rate for the plate geometry (U/H = 100 1/s); definition of a fluid with 'for any nonzero shear stress' as the chapter's reading; fluid at rest carries no shear stress; the boundary case of the ideal plastic.

sections.section: The continuum approach and the Knudsen number
sections.lecture_material: Experiments versus theoretical and computational analysis; microscopic versus macroscopic analysis; continuum approach; tray of marbles; mean free path lambda; Knudsen number lambda/L; continuum if Kn << 1.
sections.teaching_construction: Statement of the continuum hypothesis; number of molecules in air (2.446e25 per m^3); molecular spacing 3.44 nm against lambda 69 nm (factor 20) and the consequence for the tray image.

sections.section: Properties of a continuum and rate processes
sections.lecture_material: Property of the medium instead of the particle; kinematic, transport and thermodynamic classes and their members; kinematic quantities do not depend on the fluid (flow property); transport properties carry mass, momentum and energy.
sections.teaching_construction: Definition of a property as an average over a small volume; reading of the board's remark as a statement about definitions; density classed as a state property against the speaker's 'transport'; the book's definition of a rate process; unit argument that shear stress is a momentum flux.

sections.section: Mean free path and the Knudsen number in numbers
sections.lecture_material: How good is the continuum approximation: lambda for air at 300 K about 6e-8 m; lambda at 130 km about 10 m (board '102 m', speech '10.2'); 1 cm body versus 10 m aircraft.
sections.research_extension: USSA-1976: Eq. (47) and sigma = 3.65e-10 m (p. 17), Eq. (48) (p. 17), Table 10 (p. 20), Table II row at 130 km (p. 92); Liu and He (arXiv:1603.01955, p. 2) Knudsen-number regimes.
sections.teaching_construction: Kinetic derivation of lambda (swept volume; factor sqrt 2 taken from kinetic theory); checks against Table 10 (within 0.01 %) and against the 130 km row (8.75 m and 625.0/71 = 8.80 m); Table 4 of Knudsen numbers; comparison of flow length with molecular spacing for water.

sections.section: Density at a point: the volume must be neither too small nor too large
sections.lecture_material: Density as delta m over delta V; the limit delta V to 0 fails; graph of the estimate against delta V with microscopic fluctuations, a good range and material inhomogeneity; true for every property.
sections.teaching_construction: Poisson noise 1/sqrt(N); bias of a box average for a smooth density; window of box sizes (74 nm to 0.193 mm for the 1 mm gap); the window and the Knudsen number as two conditions (130 km example); Monte Carlo check in the program.

sections.section: Viscosity, the no-slip condition and Newton's law
sections.lecture_material: Viscosity as resistance to motion; two plates; ideal fluid; velocity profiles at increasing times; no-slip condition 'arises out of viscosity'; Newton's law tau = mu dVx/dy; dynamic and kinematic viscosity; table of rho, mu, nu for water, glycerin, SAE 30 oil, air; comparison of water and air.
sections.research_extension: IAPWS R12-08 viscosity of water at 293.15 K and 300 K; USSA-1976 Table 10 (air at 288.15 K); Liu and He on slip.
sections.teaching_construction: Sign convention for tau; arithmetic check mu/rho on each board row; ratios 56 and 15; shear stress mu U/H and power for the running case.

sections.section: How fast the plate drags the fluid: a diffusion equation
sections.lecture_material: The board's velocity profiles at increasing times: the plate drags more fluid with time and a fully developed profile results.
sections.teaching_construction: Slab balance from Newton's second law and Newton's law of viscosity; diffusion equation dVx/dt = nu d2Vx/dy2; series solution with verification; time scale H^2/(pi^2 nu) and 99 % time 0.4911 H^2/nu (0.573 s water, 0.0313 s air); dimensional check and its limit.

sections.section: Fluids that are not Newtonian
sections.lecture_material: Newtonian fluids as a large class (water, glycerin, oil, air); stress against strain rate: Newtonian line, ideal fluid, ideal solid, ideal plastic, curved non-Newtonian lines; analysis of non-Newtonian fluids is difficult in the course.
sections.teaching_construction: Apparent viscosity as a measure; the plate test of the Newtonian model.

sections.section: Forces on a fluid element and the stress tensor
sections.lecture_material: Newton's second law F = m a; body force per unit volume and surface force; area vector; stress as a tensor with nine components, normal and shear stresses; symmetry stated without proof; six independent components.
sections.teaching_construction: Translation of board total stress tau to T; face-first index convention; shrinking-cube symmetry derivation and face-force numerical check.

sections.section: The running case resolved
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Table 6: stress, settling time and validity for water and air at 1 mm, air at 1 um and the 10 m vehicle at 130 km; ratios 46 and 18.

sections.lecture_material: None.

sections.teaching_construction: Classification of the chapter's statements as definition, hypothesis, model or derivation under assumptions, with their boundaries.

sections.teaching_construction: Six original exercises with full solutions: derive (mean free path), compute (Knudsen number and pressure), check an assumption (Poisson model in a liquid), counterexample (a paste with a yield stress), design (density box), compute and judge (start-up wall stress in a viscometer).

sections.section: The running case and the objects of the chapter
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Running case: water at 300 K, depth 20 m behind a plane vertical wall 100 m wide; the three questions (force on a patch, stress at rest, integration); the formal model (continuum with density and stress, body and surface forces, Newton's law for an element); notation choices (bold for the board's tilde, forall for volume, Theta for temperature).

sections.section: Scalars, vectors and second-order tensors
sections.lecture_material: Scalar, vector with components and unit vectors, second-order tensor as a quantity with two directions, T_ij with nine components against three for a vector, third-order tensors mentioned and excluded.
sections.teaching_construction: Matrix layout (row = first index), component counts in two and three dimensions, the statement that the rotation law of the components is taken as given.

sections.section: The gradient of a scalar and of a vector
sections.lecture_material: Gradient of a scalar is a vector (3 components); gradient of a vector has 3 components times 3 directions and is a tensor; board layout with rows = vector component and columns = direction of differentiation (f0016).
sections.teaching_construction: Equation numbering (2.1), (2.2); simple-shear example with one nonzero entry; warning that the index convention of the velocity gradient (first index = component) differs from that of the stress (first index = face).

sections.section: Symmetric and skew-symmetric parts
sections.lecture_material: Symmetric matrix (6 independent components), skew-symmetric matrix (zero diagonal, 3 independent components), representation of a skew-symmetric tensor as a vector and the converse, A = 1/2 (A + A^T) + 1/2 (A - A^T) with proof by identity, 6 + 3 = 9.
sections.teaching_construction: Explicit axial vector xi = (-Q_yz, Q_xz, -Q_xy) with Q b = xi x b (2.3); uniqueness of the split; worked matrix with Q_xy = 2, Q_xz = -2, Q_yz = 3, xi = (-3, -2, -2) confirmed by the program.

sections.section: Forces on a fluid element: body force, surface force and the traction
sections.lecture_material: Stress is a tensor with normal (diagonal) and shear (off-diagonal) stresses, to be shown symmetric; Newton's second law dF = dm a = rho a dV; body force (gravity, electrostatic) and surface force (friction); dF_body = rho g dV; stress as force per unit area; area as a vector n |dA|; dF_surface = T . dA = (T . n)|dA|.
sections.teaching_construction: Traction t defined with the outward-normal sign convention and units (Pa); statement of why infinitely many orientations need a tensor.

sections.section: The stress tensor: faces, directions and signs
sections.lecture_material: T . n is the force per unit area; index convention (first index face, second index direction of force; board drawing of the box with x, y, z faces and T_xx, T_xy, T_xz; two-dimensional element with T_xx, T_xy, T_yx, T_yy; positive face with positive force, negative face reversed); state of stress varies from point to point and an imbalance moves the fluid.
sections.teaching_construction: Figure 2.1 (computed layout of the two-dimensional element); definition of T_ij as the j-component of the traction on the positive i face; tension and compression, p = -T_nn; tau_ij for the shear components.

sections.section: The traction on an arbitrary plane
sections.lecture_material: None (the lecture asserts T . n as the force per unit area).
sections.teaching_construction: Cauchy's relation t_j = sum_i n_i T_ij derived from a thin slab (opposite tractions) and the tetrahedron; hypotheses stated; numerical check with t = (-20, -36.67, -60) Pa, normal -71.11 Pa, shear 16.96 Pa; distinction between n . T and T . n.

sections.section: The stress tensor is symmetric
sections.lecture_material: Moment balance on a rectangle dx by dy with unit depth, (T_xy - T_yx) dx dy = I omega-dot with I = rho dx dy (dx^2 + dy^2)/12, limit dx, dy -> 0 gives T_xy = T_yx; the stress tensor is symmetric with 6 unknowns, not 9.
sections.teaching_construction: Torque about the centre with every neglected term sized (O(l^4) for the normal stresses, body force and inertia); angular acceleration 6 tau_Delta/(rho s^2) = 6.0, 602, 6.0e4 rad/s^2 for s = 1 mm, 0.1 mm, 10 micrometre with tau_Delta = 1e-3 Pa; stated assumptions (no body couples, bounded velocity gradient).

sections.section: Pressure in a fluid at rest is the same in all directions
sections.lecture_material: A stationary fluid has no shear and only a normal stress, called pressure; force balance on a wedge (x- and z-balance, p_n = p_x, p_y - p_n = rho delta_z g/2) and the limit giving Pascal's result; isotropic pressure; proven only for a stationary fluid.
sections.teaching_construction: Figure 2.2; the hypothesis stated as the definition of a fluid; second derivation from (2.6) giving T = -p I; boundary: rigid-body motion, and the Newtonian counterexample T_xx - T_yy = 4 mu kappa for plane stagnation flow (constitutive law taken as given).

sections.section: The pressure force on an element and the equation of fluid statics
sections.lecture_material: Box with pressure p and p + (dp/dx) dx on opposite faces, net force -(dp/dx) dV, dF_p = -grad p dV; the net force depends on the gradient and not on the pressure; absolute and gauge pressure, negative gauge pressure as partial vacuum; dF_p + dF_B = 0 gives grad p = rho g; scalar equations dp/dx = dp/dy = 0, dp/dz = -rho g.
sections.teaching_construction: Local form of Newton's law with the stress tensor, rho a_j = rho g_j + sum_i dT_ij/dx_i (2.10), of which (2.9) and (2.11) are special cases; units of rho g (Pa/m, 9776 Pa/m for water at 300 K); the compatibility argument that rho depends on z alone.

sections.section: Hydrostatic pressure distribution
sections.lecture_material: Integration of the three equations; p = p0 + rho g z for constant density; three layers of densities rho1, rho2, rho3 with piecewise-linear pressure and bottom value p0 + rho1 g z1 + rho2 g z2 + rho3 g z3; continuous variation of density is integrated, as in the atmosphere.
sections.teaching_construction: Depth form p = p0 + rho g h; layer thicknesses renamed d1, d2, d3; continuity of pressure across a horizontal interface by the thin-slab argument; continuous-density integral.

sections.section: When the density varies: the atmosphere and the compressibility of water
sections.lecture_material: None (the lecture states only that the atmosphere is treated by integrating with the varying density).
sections.research_extension: U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976: ideal-gas hydrostatic equation (Eqs. 1, 4, 5, p. 6), geopotential altitude (Eqs. 15, 16, p. 8), constants (Table 2, p. 2; M0, p. 9), temperature gradient -6.5 K/km' to 11 km' (Table 4, p. 3), pressure formula (Eq. 33a, p. 12), tabulated values at 0 m (p. 52) and 11000 m geometric (p. 59). IAPWS-95 Table 7 (p. 15): 300 K at 0.0992, 20.0 and 700.0 MPa.
sections.teaching_construction: Density change gH/w^2 = 8.7e-5 at the wall; test of Delta rho = Delta p/w^2 against the table (0.886 % against 0.878 %); atmosphere check: closed form and trapezoid integration give 22,700 Pa and 0.36480 kg/m^3 against 22,699 Pa and 0.36480 kg/m^3 in the table; constant density gives -30,591 Pa with g_0' = 9.80665 and H_gp = 10,981 m' (-30,865 Pa with g = 9.81 m/s^2 and z = 11,000 m); mean density 0.730 kg/m^3 (59.6 % of sea level).

sections.section: The manometer
sections.lecture_material: U-tube manometer with bulb A, points B, C, D, E, O, three fluids rho1, rho2, air, heights h1 to h4; the four pressure relations; p_A = p_atm + rho_air g h4 + rho2 g h3 - rho1 g h1 - rho2 g h2; with rho2 >> rho1, rho_air and rho1 ~ rho_air, p_A ~ p_atm + rho2 g (h3 - h2); gauge pressure rho2 g (h3 - h2).
sections.research_extension: Sea-level air density 1.225 kg/m^3 (U.S. Standard Atmosphere Table I, p. 52).
sections.teaching_construction: Geometry read from the board relations; validity conditions (connected columns, constant density, continuity across interfaces, no capillarity); example with water and air, exact 1957.65 Pa against 1955.24 Pa (0.12 %); criterion on the neglected term.

sections.section: Hydrostatic force on a submerged surface
sections.lecture_material: Free surface, p = p_atm + rho g h with h ~ -z, dF = -rho g h dA, F_R = -rho g integral h dA, components F_x = rho g integral h dA_x and F_z = rho g integral h dA_z with projected areas, interpretation as the weight of the prism of fluid.
sections.teaching_construction: Sign and normal made explicit; condition for dropping p_atm; geometric reading (horizontal force = force on the vertical projection, vertical force = weight of the water above); wall result (2.20) 1.955e8 N; Figure 2.3.

sections.section: The centre of pressure of a plane surface
sections.lecture_material: Point of action of the resultant by equating moments, like the centre of gravity; centre of pressure; the flat plate left as a home assignment, a curved object harder.
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation of F = rho g h_c A and s_cp = s_c + I_c/(s_c A) with the parallel-axis theorem; checks: wall 2H/3 (13.33 m) and moment 1.30e9 N m; gate 117.3 kN at 2.1667 m; curved surfaces excluded.

sections.section: Buoyancy and Archimedes' principle
sections.lecture_material: 3-D object of volume V submerged; pressure force on the upper surface rho g V_u and on the lower surface rho g V_b; net rho g (V_b - V_u) = rho g V; Archimedes' principle; balloon in equilibrium when weight equals buoyancy and rises when buoyancy is larger.
sections.research_extension: Sea-level air density (Standard Atmosphere Table I, p. 52) for the 1 m^3 example (12.02 N with g = 9.81).
sections.teaching_construction: Conditions of the prism argument; divergence-theorem derivation F_b = -integral rho g dV for variable density with the line of action through the centre of mass of the displaced fluid; boundaries (sealed base, floating body); sphere check 40.9508 N against 40.9505 N.

sections.section: Executable check of the algebra and the running case
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.research_extension: Standard Atmosphere and IAPWS values as the inputs of checks 8 and 9.
sections.teaching_construction: NumPy program with nine checks (sym/skew split and axial vector; traction and the non-symmetric product test; net force on a cube in a linear stress field against the divergence; angular acceleration table; wall and gate by numerical integration; sphere buoyancy by surface integration; manometer; atmosphere closed form and trapezoid integration; compressibility of water); printed output compared byte for byte; two failure tests described and run.

sections.section: The running case resolved
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Table 2.1 of the wall quantities; the wall inclined at 60 degrees (A = 2309 m^2, F = 2.258e8 N normal, 1.955e8 N horizontal, 1.129e8 N vertical equal to the weight of the water above) as a test of the geometric reading of (2.19).

sections.section: What the chapter establishes and what it does not
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Classification of the assumptions (model, idealization, approximation) and of the places where each fails (media with internal angular momentum, moving viscous fluids, gases over kilometres, water at tens of MPa, absent fluid under a body, curved surfaces, accelerated tanks).

sections.section: Exercises
sections.lecture_material: Exercise 3 uses the plate calculation the lecture assigned as homework; Exercise 4 tests the statement of Archimedes' principle.
sections.research_extension: Exercises 1 to 6 use the sea-level air density and the IAPWS water density.
sections.teaching_construction: Six original exercises with full solutions: compute and check a convention (traction and the two products), check an assumption (accelerated tank), compute and design (gate and hinge), counterexample (sealed cylinder), check an assumption and design (manometer with a dense bulb liquid), derive (divergence form of buoyancy and its moment, two-layer prism).

sections.section: The running case and the objects of the chapter
sections.lecture_material: None.
sections.teaching_construction: Fluid element, path, velocity field and property field as the formal model; running case in three parts (A the wind that turns, from the lecture's field; B the sheared wind with gamma-dot = 0.1 1/s; C the nozzle with Q = 0.2 L/s, 16 mm to 4 mm over 30 mm); notation of the board (V_x, V_y, V_z, D/Dt) and its relation to Stokes's u, v, w.

sections.section: Two descriptions of a flow: following an element and watching a point
sections.lecture_material: Eulerian observer at a place and Lagrangian observer on an element (traffic analogy: reporter at the gate and the marked red car); the speaker's two judgments (Eulerian preferred because of the number of elements; basic laws more amenable to the Lagrangian description); labelling of an element by (x0, y0, z0, t0).
sections.teaching_construction: Path map X(x0, t0; t) with three arguments; equation (3.1) as the definition of the Eulerian velocity field and as the path equation; property record eta_L; worked example of the sheared wind with check against (3.1); the two judgments attributed to the speaker.

sections.section: The material derivative
sections.lecture_material: Chain-rule derivation from the total differential of eta(x, y, z, t); D eta/Dt = d eta/dt + V.grad eta; names total/material, local and convective; applied to the velocity (total or material, local and convective acceleration) and written in components; the speed-breaker road (steady flow, nonzero material derivative).
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation by the chain rule along the path; balloon example (10 m/s, 2 K per 100 km, 0.72 K/h); Table 3.1 of four fields (steady and unsteady, with and without material acceleration), including V = x/(1+t) with a Lagrangian check; average acceleration over a distance, (V2^2 - V1^2)/(2 l) = -4.5 m/s2 for 60 to 10 km/h over an assumed 30 m.

sections.section: Steady and unsteady flow, and the choice of frame
sections.lecture_material: Steady flow: d/dt of V, p, T equal to zero everywhere; D/Dt may not be zero for a steady flow; steady versus unsteady depends on the frame (boat in a river, observer on the shore and observer moving with the boat); choose the frame carefully.
sections.teaching_construction: Transformation (3.7) to a frame of constant velocity u_f, proof that the local derivative changes by (u_f.grad)V and the material acceleration does not (3.8, 3.9); characterization of flows that are steady in some constant-velocity frame as rigidly translating patterns; limits (constant-velocity frames only; a real wake is only approximately a rigid pattern).

sections.section: Pathlines, streamlines, streaklines and stream tubes
sections.lecture_material: Pathline (trajectory of an element, Lagrangian; tracer particles, hydrogen bubbles from an electrode); streamline (instantaneous, tangent to V, Eulerian; dr x V = 0 with its three component equations and dy/dx = Vy/Vx in 2-D; flow cannot cross a streamline); stream tube and conservation of volume flow rate; streakline (locus of tracer particles at an instant, smoke from a chimney; more common in experiments).
sections.teaching_construction: Table 3.2 (which elements, which times); path equation (3.10); stream-tube argument with the divergence theorem (3.15), assuming incompressible flow for equal instantaneous volume flux; steady flow guarantees that a fixed tube wall remains impermeable, while an unsteady fixed-direction field can also have this property; nozzle numbers (0.995 and 15.9 m/s, 5.07e4 m/s2 at the exit, transit 13.2 ms, 11 degree half-angle) with the one-dimensional approximation stated; streakline definition (3.16).

sections.section: A flow in which the three lines differ
sections.lecture_material: Velocity field 1 i + 0 j for t <= 5 s and cos45 i + sin45 j for t > 5 s; streamlines before and after 5 s; the field is unsteady; pathlines of elements released at intervals of 1 s up to 10 s; streaklines at 10 s and at 9 s; all three lines differ; streaklines easier in experiments; for a steady flow the three lines are identical.
sections.teaching_construction: Closed forms (3.18) for the paths; streakline at 10 s as a horizontal piece at 3.54 m and a 45-degree piece (5 m each), general t; Figure 3.1; comparison of the three curves through P0 (bends at (5,0) and (3.54,3.54), 3.83 m apart); proof that the three lines coincide in a steady flow (autonomous equation); counterexample to the converse (V = (f(t), 0)); program check.

sections.section: How a fluid element moves and deforms
sections.lecture_material: Rectangular element ABCD in a 2-D field Vx i + Vy j; corner velocities by Taylor expansion; element after dt; translation, rotation, shear (angular) deformation, dilatation (dilation, extension); the sketched element combines all four.
sections.teaching_construction: First-order validity condition (element small against the length of change of the gradients); edge vectors after dt (3.20).

sections.section: Rotation rate and vorticity
sections.lecture_material: Rotation rate of the element as the average of the rotation rates of edges AB and AD; Omega_z = (1/2)(dVy/dx - dVx/dy); Omega_x and Omega_y by symmetry; curl of V and its components; vorticity omega = curl V; Omega = (1/2) omega; in solid mechanics a load rotates an element to a final state, in a fluid the rotation continues.
sections.research_extension: Stokes (1845), Art. 2, eq. (1), p. 81: angular velocities of the fluid with the factor 1/2, and his remark that they coincide with rigid-body angular velocities for solid motion.
sections.teaching_construction: Signed counterclockwise convention for both edge angles (3.21); checks on rigid rotation and the sheared wind (Omega_z = -0.05 1/s, omega_z = -0.10 1/s); cyclic permutation giving (3.23); the factor 2 between omega and Omega stated as a warning.

sections.section: Irrotational flow and the meaning of rotation
sections.lecture_material: Irrotational flow: omega = 0 everywhere; an element along a streamline of an irrotational flow keeps its orientation, in a rotational flow it turns; circular streamlines can be rotational or irrotational (Earth around the Sun; element turning once per revolution).
sections.teaching_construction: Rigid rotation (omega_z = 2 Omega_0) and free vortex (3.26) as the two circular-streamline flows; derivation of the turning of the radial and tangential line elements (-c/r^2 and +c/r^2) and of the shear strain rate -c/r^2 (program: -0.8 1/s at r^2 = 1.25 m2); precise meaning of 'maintains its orientation' (average rotation; principal-axis lines turn at Omega_z).

sections.section: Shear strain rate
sections.lecture_material: Angle BAD -> B'A'D', 90 deg -> 90 deg - (d theta1 + d theta2); shear deformation rate epsilon_xy = (1/2)(d theta1/dt - d theta2/dt) = (1/2)(dVy/dx + dVx/dy), epsilon_xz and epsilon_yz by symmetry; in solid mechanics the deformation, in fluid mechanics the rate.
sections.teaching_construction: Angle between the edges 90 deg + theta2 - theta1 with signed angles; factor 1/2 explained (entry of the tensor; the full rate 2 epsilon_xy is the engineering shear strain rate); checks on rigid rotation and the sheared wind; rates are instantaneous (45 deg after 10 s, not 1 rad).

sections.section: Extensional strain rate and the strain-rate tensor
sections.lecture_material: Extensional strain rate epsilon_xx = rate of extension of edge AB against its original length = dVx/dx, epsilon_yy, epsilon_zz; strain-rate tensor with nine components, symmetric, six independent (three direct, three shear).
sections.teaching_construction: Edge length to first order in dt; area and volume rate of change, epsilon_xx + epsilon_yy + epsilon_zz = div V (3.30), zero for density preserved by each element, including spatially nonuniform density (mass-conservation relation taken as given); full matrix (3.31); exact reason for the symmetry (both entries are half the rate of change of the angle between the same two edges).

sections.section: The velocity gradient splits into a strain rate and a rotation
sections.lecture_material: Gradient of V as the 3 x 3 matrix of derivatives; split into symmetric part (equal to the strain-rate tensor) and skew-symmetric part (entries -Omega_z, Omega_y, -Omega_x); no force used, pure kinematics; uniform flow gives zero gradient.
sections.research_extension: Stokes (1845), Art. 2, pp. 80-84: relative velocities split into a part from angular velocities and a symmetric remainder; axes of extension (p. 82); motion compounded of translation, rotation, uniform dilatation and two shifting motions (pp. 83-84).
sections.teaching_construction: Derivation of material-line stretching and turning from the velocity gradient, written in the chapter's own steps and not offered as a new result; W n = Omega cross n; principal-direction turning; mean turning of two perpendicular lines and their angular narrowing, with advected-line checks. Trace defined at first use.

sections.section: A fluid element near a wall
